paragraphs: §1 — Gen 9:6: the verse commands the execution of murderers, not the soul's passage through human forms

A group of them [the metempsychosists] have found a foothold in things from Scripture which they fancied contained that which indicates the soundness of their doctrine. Among them is His saying [Gen 9:6] שׁוֹפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ etc. ("whoever sheds the blood of the man, by the man shall his blood be shed"). They claimed that He stated in this that whoever sheds the blood of a human being has his own blood shed while he is in the form of human beings — and that He thereby indicated that the man who shed the blood may [at the time of his crime] have been in other than the form of human beings, save that he is not put to death by that killing except while he is in the form of a human being, just as he had killed while in the form of a human being. We have already spoken to that in our commentary on בְּרֵאשִׁית: that this is only a command to people that they should put to death everyone who has killed a human being; and His saying בָּאָדָם ("by the man") means by the human being — "his blood is shed," that is, "I have made it obligatory upon human beings that they put him to death."

: The opening prooftext and Q's method in miniature. The transmigrationists read ba-adam ("by the man") distributively — "in [the state of being] a man" — to wring from Gen 9:6 the premise that the murderer, having shed blood in some prior bodily incarnation, is requited only once he has migrated back into human form. Q dissolves it grammatically: ba-adam is the instrumental by/through a human being — i.e., the verse delegates the execution to human agents ("I have made it obligatory upon human beings that they put him to death"), the standard Karaite construal grounding capital jurisdiction in the verse. The back-reference is to Q's Torah commentary (Kitāb al-Riyāḍ wa-l-Ḥadāʾiq), here under its Bereshit section. The absence of an Arabic section marker on this run marks it as the preamble; Nemoy's first numeral (§2) falls on the next prooftext.
§2 — Lev 11:43: "you shall be defiled by them" is mere emphasis, or refers to the sin of eating

2. And among them is His saying [Lev 11:43] וְלֹא תִטַּמְּאוּ בָּהֶם וְנִטְמֵתֶם בָּם ("you shall not make yourselves unclean by them, and so be defiled by them"). They claimed that He meant: if you eat of them and become polluted by them, I defile you into them — that is, I set your souls into them, so that you become punished within them. But this is only a repetition in the wording; its meaning is: do not make a practice of eating them, so coming to intend the defilement by them, whereby their uncleanness comes to inhere in you. And that is the counterpart of His saying [Deut 5:? / parallel] וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים ("and you shall be holy"). And it is admissible that this refers to the [matter of] transgression — that is, that when you have defiled yourselves by them through eating, you have [thereby] sinned by them — the counterpart of His saying [Exod 28:38] מַחֲלַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל etc., the interpretation of which is His saying [Exod 28:38] וְהָיָה עַל מִצְחוֹ … אֶת כָּל עֲוֺנֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("he shall bear all the iniquities of the Children of Israel").

: The transmigrationists read ve-nitmetem bam ("and be defiled by/in them") as locative — your souls are lodged within the unclean creatures as punishment. Q offers two non-metempsychotic readings: (a) the clause is mere rhetorical emphasis (takrīr fī al-qawl) — "do not defile yourselves … and [so] be defiled," a pleonasm reinforcing the prohibition; (b) "be defiled" = "incur sin," on the model of maḥalat / ʿavon (Exod 28:38), where bearing impurity is bearing guilt. The וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים citation: the source pointer reads `בשם, מ' [= דב' ה']`, a corrupted reference; the phrase "and you shall be holy" recurs in Lev 11:44-45 (the immediate context) and is glossed in the source as the converse of the defilement clause. The Exod 28:38 pairing (the high priest "bears the iniquity") fixes tum'ah = culpability.
§3 — Josh 9 / Hos 9:10: men who become "abominations" denotes their becoming defiled by sin, not the lodging of souls in unclean beasts

3. And of that is His saying concerning the Children of Israel [in the affair of the Gibeonites], [Josh 9:14] וַיִּקְחוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים מִצֵּידָם … and וַיִּהְיוּ שִׁקּוּצִים — "[that they] became abominations." [Here the OCR is corrupt; Q quotes the phrase in which the men "became abominations" (shiqquṣim).] They claimed that He meant that the Children of Israel, when they sinned by taking [from their provisions], perished and became filth — by their souls being set into the bodies of the beast that is שֶׁקֶץ ("an abomination"). But he intended by this only the counterpart of what preceded it from His saying [Lev 11:43] וְנִטְמֵאתֶם בָּם — namely that He has forbidden them transgressions and informed them that whenever they should oppose [Him] and sin, they would become filthy and unclean; for His saying [Hos 9:10] תְּשַׁקְּצוּ אֶת נַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם etc. ("you shall make your souls abominable") confirms that. His saying כְּאָהֳבָם ("according to their love") supports it — that is, that they loved to be abominations, and so became thus; he did not mean that they loved to be in the bodies of the abominable beast.

: The men who "became shiqquṣim" (abominations) are read by the opponents as souls relocated into the bodies of sheqeṣ-creatures (the swarming things of Lev 11). Q again normalizes: to "become an abomination" is to become morally defiled by sin, parallel to Lev 11:43, and sealed by Hos 9:10 (teshaqqeṣu et nafshotekhem, "you make your souls abominable" — souls defiled, not relocated). The clinching word is ke-ohovam ("according to their love," Hos 9:10): they loved to be abominable and so became so — a moral act of will, not a post-mortem transmigration. The Josh 9:14 citation (the Gibeonite-provisions episode) is partly garbled in the OCR (`מצ...` / `שקצים באת...`, with the multimodal output breaking off); the consonantal frame "the men took of their provisions … and became abominations" is secure from the surrounding Arabic, and is flagged for the edition. The Hos 9:10 verse is the load-bearing prooftext-turned-counter-prooftext.
§4 — Ps 49:12: qirbam batteimo is "their grave," not the soul's perpetual house

4. And of that is His saying [Ps 49:12] קִרְבָּם בָּתֵּימוֹ לְעוֹלָם מִשְׁכְּנֹתָם ("their inward thought is that their houses are forever, their dwelling-places [to all generations]"). They claimed that he means that the sinners' insides — that is, their bodies — are houses for them throughout time; meaning that their souls do not part from the bodies, but are transferred from body to body until the end of time, since transgressions had so abounded in them that they are not refined [enough] to deserve release. But Scripture did not say "the insides of others," which are [all] the rest of the bodies; rather it said their own insides. Now if the statement be on its surface, then it would have to be that their bodies abide forever — and this is false. The meaning of קִרְבָּם בָּתֵּימוֹ is rather קִבְרָם ("their grave"); and that is like כֶּבֶשׂ / כֶּשֶׂב, שִׂמְלָה / שַׂלְמָה [the metathesized doublets]. For he reported only that, in the death of punishment, they are abiding and enduring — and that is according to what we expounded in the discussion of reward and punishment. His mention of the grave is by the running custom that graves are the houses of the dead, [spoken] absolutely.

: A double move — philological and contextual. The transmigrationists read qirbam batteimo le-ʿolam ("their inward part / their houses forever") as: the sinners' bodies are perpetual houses for their souls, which migrate body-to-body endlessly because too sin-laden to win release. Q's reply: (1) the verse speaks of their own insides, which on the literal reading would absurdly entail bodies abiding forever; (2) the true sense of qirbam is qivram, "their grave," by the well-attested Hebrew consonantal metathesis — Q adduces the standard grammarians' doublets keves/keseb ("lamb") and simlah/salmah ("garment"), in which the order of consonants is transposed without change of sense. So the verse means the wicked's grave is their eternal house — "the death of punishment" in which they abide — on the ordinary idiom that the grave is "the house of the dead." The back-reference is to Q's treatment of al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb (reward and punishment) in the preceding eschatological babs (M3 B7–12; see glossary §VI).
§5 — Jer 17:13 and Ps 90:3: "written in the earth" and "You turn man back" concern the land of punishment and moral admonition, not recycling through bodies

5. And like that, they clung to His saying [Jer 17:13] וְסוּרַי בָּאָרֶץ יִכָּתֵבוּ ("and those who turn away from me shall be written in the earth"), [claiming] that He reported that those who deviate and turn aside from Him and from His obedience are "written in the earth," and that this is by way of the recurrence (al-karr) through bodies, body after body. But the statement on this is like the statement on what preceded: namely that they are written in the land of death, which is the land of punishment.

And of that is His saying [Ps 90:3] תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד דַּכָּא וַתֹּאמֶר שׁוּבוּ בְנֵי אָדָם ("You turn man back to contrition, and say, 'Return, O children of men'"). They claimed that its meaning is that You [repeatedly] bring the human being back until he is purified and refined — that is, You cycle him through bodies. But the meaning in this is that He intended: You turn the human being back and restrain him with command and prohibition until he obeys and is purified and refined; for he explained it by his saying תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד דַּכָּא ("You turn man back to contrition"), and that is according to what we said — that You only cycle them back by saying to them שׁוּבוּ בְנֵי אָדָם ("Return, O children of men").

: Two prooftexts of "turning/returning." (1) Jer 17:13 ve-suray ba-areṣ yikkatevu ("those who turn from me shall be written in the earth") is read as the soul's karr (cyclical recurrence) through earthly bodies; Q refers it instead to "the land of death/punishment" (the eschatological reading he just used for Ps 49:12). (2) Ps 90:3 tashev enosh ʿad dakka ("You turn man back to contrition / to being crushed") is read as God's recycling of man through bodies until purified; Q reads tashev morally — God "turns man back" by admonition (command, prohibition, the call "Return, O children of men"), so the "turning" is repentance under exhortation, not metempsychosis. The verse's own parallel hemistich (va-tomer shuvu, "and You say, Return") supplies the gloss: the turning is effected by speech, i.e., by the prophetic summons to repent.
§6 — Ps 90:3 again, and va-tashov nefesh: the soul's "return" is restored well-being, the prophet's plea is for prosperity, not re-embodiment

6. And like that they claimed in his saying [Ps 90:3] תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד דַּכָּא שׁוּבוּ — [that is] that He cycles my soul from body to body; and this "returning" of the soul is as he said [Lam 5:21 / cf. Ps] בִּימֵי קֶדֶם וְלֹא דֻכְּאוּ עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה ("as in days of old, and they were not crushed until this day"). But what the prophet sought from God (mighty and exalted) is only [the return] by way of the felicities — such as the wisdom of which it is said that it וַתָּשָׁב נֶפֶשׁ ("restores the soul" [Ps 19:8]), and ease, and satiety from good things — like [1 Sam 30:12] … וַתָּשָׁב רוּחוֹ אֵלָיו ("and his spirit returned to him"; reading with the figure of the famished man who ate and revived: נָשָׂא … יָדוֹ וַיָּבֹא וַיֹּאכַל וַתָּשָׁב רוּחוֹ אֵלָיו). And the opposite of that is misery in the land, on account of his saying [Job 5:3 / cf.] בְּאֹהֶב שֹׁרֶשׁ … לֹא יִתְכּוֹנֵן וְיָשַׁב רוּחִי etc. And the like of that is much.

: The §6 cluster turns on the verb √šwb ("return/restore") and its noun-object nefesh / ruaḥ. The opponents read every "return of the soul/spirit" as a soul re-entering a body. Q shows that teshuvat ha-nefesh in Scripture is the restoration of well-being: wisdom "restores the soul" (Ps 19:8 meshivat nefesh), and the famished man's "spirit returns to him" once he eats (1 Sam 30:12 — David's reviving of the abandoned Egyptian). So "the soul returns" = a person is revived/restored to vigour or wisdom, the very thing the psalmist prays for; the antonym is "misery in the land." The citation pointers in this section are heavily OCR-damaged (the consonantal frames va-tashov nefesh, va-tashov ruḥo elav, be-ohev shoresh … ve-yashav ruḥi are secure from the multimodal output; the precise book/chapter pointers — Lam 5:21? Ps 19:8? 1 Sam 30:12? Job? — are reconstructed from the lemmata and flagged for the edition).
§7 — Job 14:14: "until my change comes" is the natural close of life, not a change of bodies

7. And like that is the saying of Job [Job 14:14] כָּל יְמֵי צְבָאִי אֲקַוֶּה עַד בּוֹא חֲלִיפָתִי ("all the days of my appointed service I will wait, until my change comes"). They claimed that he meant my exchange — intending [exchange] from body to body. But the meaning in this is that he said: all the days of my standing-fast — that is, in the world — until there comes the time of my passing, meaning his passing from the world; like His saying [1 Kgs 18:? / cf.] בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה … הַגֶּשֶׁם חָלַף הָלַךְ לוֹ ("the rain passed and was gone"), [where ḥalaf] means "passed away." And that is the counterpart of His saying [Ps 102:27] כַּלְּבוּשׁ תַּחֲלִיפֵם וְיַחֲלֹפוּ ("like a garment You change them, and they pass away"), [meaning] like a garment You cause them to pass and they pass away — for he had put forward the mention of wearing-out [decay], by his saying [Ps 102:27] וְכֻלָּם כַּבֶּגֶד יִבְלוּ etc. ("and they all wear out like a garment").

: Job 14:14 ʿad bo ḥalifati ("until my change/relief comes") is the classic transmigration prooftext: ḥalifah = "exchange [of body]." Q reads ḥalifah as the passing away of the natural lifespan: "all the days of my [appointed] service I wait, until the time of my departure from the world." He grounds the sense of √ḥlf = "pass away / pass on" in (a) ha-geshem ḥalaf halakh lo, "the rain passed and was gone," and (b) Ps 102:26-27, where ka-levush taḥalifem ve-yaḥalofu ("like a garment You change them and they pass") is preceded by ve-khullam ka-beged yivlu ("they all wear out like a garment") — so √ḥlf there is the perishing of the worn-out garment, not its re-wearing. The 1 Kgs/rain citation pointer is garbled (`בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים` in the source — "in three days," apparently a conflation); the operative lemma ha-geshem ḥalaf halakh lo is secure and is the controlling proof for √ḥlf = "pass away."
§8 — Job 38:14: titthappekh ke-ḥomer ḥotam is said of the earth, not the soul

8. And of that is His saying [Job 38:14] תִּתְהַפֵּךְ כְּחֹמֶר חוֹתָם וְיִתְיַצְּבוּ כְּמוֹ לְבוּשׁ ("it is turned like clay [under] the seal, and they stand forth like a garment"). They made this to be said of the soul; but it is in fact said of the earth, for He said [Job 38:13] לֶאֱחֹז בְּכַנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ ("to take hold of the corners of the earth"). So He said that it [the earth] turns about with them in torment, like the clay of the seal, and that they are set up upon it as though they were a garment for it, unable to part from it.

: A simple mis-assignment of the grammatical subject. Titthappekh ke-ḥomer ḥotam ("it turns like clay under the seal," Job 38:14) is read by the opponents as said of the soul (the soul "turning/transforming" — re-impressed like clay into new bodily forms). Q points to the immediately preceding verse, Job 38:13 le-eḥoz be-khanfot ha-areṣ ("to take hold of the corners of the earth"): the subject is the earth, dawn-light revolving it like clay under a seal-stamp, with its inhabitants "standing forth like a garment" upon it — bound to it, unable to part from it. The figure is of the earth and its dwellers, not of a transmigrating soul.
§9 — The promise-and-threat passages: collective and national, not individual reincarnation

9. And they may cling to the account of [Lev 26:3] בְּחֻקֹּתַי [תֵּלֵכוּ] ("if you walk in my statutes"), and the account of [Deut 11:13 / cf.] דַּבֵּר … וְיָשֻׁבוּ and וְהָיָה עֵקֶב תִּשְׁמְעוּן ("and it shall come to pass, because you hearken"), and what He promised the righteous of the kinds of bliss, and what He threatened the wicked with of the kinds of affliction in this world — whereas we see the matter [running] contrary to that, [namely] from the standpoint of sense-perception, together with what the prophets have reported of that, such as His saying [Jer 12:1] מַדּוּעַ דֶּרֶךְ רְשָׁעִים צָלֵחָה etc. ("why does the way of the wicked prosper?") and the like. They said: were it not that deeds had gone before for the righteous, by which they deserved that affliction, it would not have befallen them; and likewise, were it not that the wicked had good deeds gone before, those favours would not have reached them — and that is according to what we said [they hold] regarding a dwelling [i.e., a prior life] before this one. But as for the statement on the account of [Lev 26:3] בְּחֻקֹּתַי [introduced by] בּוֹעַז [?], and the account of נָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא, and וְהָיָה עֵקֶב תִּשְׁמְעוּן — that does not refer to individuals of the people, but rather aims at the whole and the generality; and we shall expound that in its [proper] place.

: The opponents' strongest empirical argument: the Torah's blessing-and-curse passages (Lev 26 be-ḥuqqotai; Deut 7:12 / 11:13 ve-hayah ʿeqev tishmaʿun) promise this-worldly reward for obedience and affliction for sin — yet experience contradicts this (the wicked prosper: Jer 12:1 maddua derekh reshaʿim ṣaleḥah). The metempsychosists explain the mismatch by prior lives: the suffering righteous are paying for past-life sins, the prospering wicked are collecting on past-life merits — "a dwelling before this one." Q's reply (developed in §10) is twofold: the blessing-curse passages are addressed to the collective (the nation as a whole), not to individuals, so they do not promise per-individual desert in this life; full treatment is deferred "to its place." The OCR garbles the citation-frame badly here — `בּוֹעַז אִם בְּחֻקּוֹתַי` and `נדב וְאֲבִיהוּא` are intrusive/conflated pointers (Boaz; Nadab-and-Abihu) whose connection to be-ḥuqqotai is unclear in the damaged text; reconstructed conservatively and flagged.
§10 — The prophet's own astonishment refutes transmigration; the saints' fear of death is answered on our doctrine, not theirs

10. As for what they mentioned of the saying of the prophet [Jer 12:1] מַדּוּעַ דֶּרֶךְ רְשָׁעִים צָלֵחָה etc. ("why does the way of the wicked prosper?") and the like of it — we have already given the answer to that in the discussion of reward and punishment, that being where we mentioned the saying of שְׁלֹמֹה [Solomon, i.e., Qohelet] [Eccl 8:14] אֲשֶׁר יֵשׁ צַדִּיקִים שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ אֲלֵיהֶם כְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָרְשָׁעִים וְיֵשׁ רְשָׁעִים שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ אֲלֵיהֶם כְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַצַּדִּיקִים etc. ("there are righteous men to whom it happens according to the work of the wicked, and there are wicked men to whom it happens according to the work of the righteous").

Moreover, that which they clung to of the prophet's saying, and what he asked about, recoils upon them. For it is to be said to them: if the cause of that [prosperity of the wicked and affliction of the righteous] is the recurrence [through bodies], and if what occurred of the safety of the wicked and the affliction of the righteous was only on account of deeds that had gone before for them in a dwelling before this one — then the prophet ought to have been better-informed of that than you. So why did he deny it, and marvel at it, and ask about its cause? And in this is a refutation of what they claim of transmigration (al-tanāsukh); for had that been as they say, the prophets would have known it, and we would not have needed to ask about it.

And they may cling to what we have already mentioned of the aversion of the prophets and the saints to death — but this is binding upon them rather than upon us. For if the saints had known that, after death, they would pass to another body in which they would enjoy bliss and delight, they would not have been averse to it; whereas we have [already] reported the cause of that on our [own] doctrine.

: The bab's closing coup. Q presses the metempsychotic explanation of theodicy (prior-life desert explains present prosperity/affliction) against itself with two arguments. (1) An argument from prophetic ignorance: if reincarnation were the standing explanation, the prophets — Jeremiah (Jer 12:1), Qohelet (Eccl 8:14) — would know it and not marvel at the prosperity of the wicked and ask its cause; their very astonishment proves the doctrine false. The cross-reference is to Q's earlier treatment of theodicy under al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb (reward and punishment, M3 B7–12), where the prosperity-of-the-wicked problem was handled via deferred eschatological recompense. (2) A tu quoque on the saints' fear of death: the opponents adduce the prophets' aversion to death as evidence (for them, presumably, that death is a fall into a lower body); Q turns it — on their premises the saints should welcome death as passage to a blissful next body, so their fear refutes transmigration; whereas Q's own doctrine (resurrection-and-recompense, not recurrence) accounts for the fear consistently. The name al-tanāsukh (metempsychosis) is named explicitly here for the first time in the bab.

- The bab's subject and adversary. Bab 18 refutes the transmigration of souls (al-tanāsukh, named explicitly at §10; the doctrine of al-karr — the soul's "recurrence" through successive bodies — at §5). The heading, fī-mā taʿallaqū bihi min al-kitāb wa-raddihi ("on that to which they clung from Scripture, and its refutation"), uses the same taʿallaqū ("they found a foothold / clung") idiom Q used for the Christian prooftexts in Bab 6 — signalling that this bab is the scriptural-refutation half of the metempsychosis treatment, following Bab 17's exposition of the doctrine and (presumably) its rational refutation. The adversaries are the aṣḥāb al-tanāsukh; within the Anwār's sectarian frame these are most plausibly the metempsychotic current Q associates with ʿAnan/the early sectarians or with a philosophical (Pythagorean-Platonic, via the falāsifa and the Ismāʿīlī/ghulāt milieu) reincarnationism circulating in 10th-c. Iraq.

- The method is uniform and philological. Every prooftext is dissolved by one of three moves, exactly as in Bab 6: (a) a grammatical reading (ba-adam = "by a human being," §1; qirbam = qivram "their grave" by consonantal metathesis, §4), (b) a figurative/idiomatic reading (defilement = sin, §§2–3; "return of the soul" = restored vigour, §6; ḥalifah = death/passing, §7), or (c) a context reading that re-assigns the verse's referent (the subject of Job 38:14 is the earth, not the soul, §8; the blessing-curse passages are collective, not individual, §9). The controlling axiom is the same priority of the plain/contextual sense (ẓāhir) that Q wields against both Christian typology and Rabbanite midrash.

- The metathesis argument (§4) is the philological showpiece: qirbam ("their inward part") is to be read qivram ("their grave"), justified by the recognized Hebrew doublets keves/keseb ("lamb," Lev–Deut) and simlah/salmah ("garment"), where consonantal order transposes without semantic change. This is a standard medieval Hebraist observation (the √QRB ~ √QBR link is exploited by later grammarians and exegetes); Q's use of it to defuse Ps 49:12 is exegetically deft and turns the transmigrationists' prooftext into a verse about the grave as the wicked's eternal "house."

- The theodicy hinge (§§9–10). The genuinely difficult prooftext is not lexical but empirical: the Torah's this-worldly blessing-and-curse promises clash with the observed prosperity of the wicked (Jer 12:1; Eccl 8:14), and metempsychosis offers a tidy theodicy (prior-life desert). Q's two replies are characteristic: the blessing-curse passages are collective/national (so they make no per-individual this-life promise), and — the sharper point — the prophets' own astonishment at the prosperity of the wicked proves they did not hold the reincarnationist explanation, which would have dissolved the puzzle. The whole problem is referred back to Q's eschatological treatment of al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb (deferred otherworldly recompense), the doctrine that does Q's theodicy-work in place of tanāsukh.

- The tu quoque on the fear of death (§10 end) mirrors the dialectical reversals of Bab 6 (the yikkaret trap; the ʿarel trap): the opponents' own datum (the saints' aversion to death) is turned against them — on their premises the saints should welcome death — while Q's resurrection-recompense doctrine accommodates the datum.
